[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Model Quantization (PTQ, QAT) and Pruning"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"As deep learning models grow in size, deploying them to resource-constrained edge devices becomes increasingly challenging. Model optimization techniques such as Post-Training Quantization (PTQ), Quantization-Aware Training (QAT), and Pruning are essential tools for reducing memory footprint, lowering latency, and maintaining high prediction accuracy."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Understanding Model Quantization"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"Quantization converts model weights and activations from high-precision formats (like 32-bit floating-point, FP32) to lower-precision formats (like 8-bit integers, INT8). This dramatically speeds up arithmetic operations on modern hardware accelerators while reducing the model size by up to 75%."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"FP32: Standard training precision, 4 bytes per parameter."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"FP16/BF16: Half precision, widely used in mixed-precision training."},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"INT8: Quantized integer representation, 1 byte per parameter, optimized for edge inference."},{"order":8,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ)"},{"order":9,"type":"paragraph","text":"PTQ is applied to an already trained and converged floating-point model. It requires no retraining, making it fast and easy to implement. A small representative calibration dataset is passed through the network to determine the optimal scaling factors for mapping floating-point ranges to integer ranges."},{"order":10,"type":"code","text":"import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# Define a simple floating-point model
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Conv2d(3, 16, kernel_size=3),
    nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(16, 10)
)
model.eval()

# Apply Post-Training Static Quantization
backend = "qnnpack"
model.qconfig = torch.quantization.get_default_qconfig(backend)
torch.quantization.prepare(model, inplace=True)
# Run calibration with representative data here
torch.quantization.convert(model, inplace=True)"},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"3. Quantization-Aware Training (QAT)"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"While PTQ is fast, it can cause accuracy drops in highly sensitive or compact models. QAT simulates quantization effects during the training phase itself. Fake-quantization modules are inserted into the graph to model rounding errors during the forward pass, allowing the optimizer to adjust weights to compensate for the lower precision."},{"order":13,"type":"code","text":"# Prepare model for Quantization-Aware Training
model.train()
model.qconfig = torch.quantization.get_default_qat_qconfig("fbgemm")
torch.quantization.prepare_qat(model, inplace=True)

# Standard training loop follows
# optimizer.step(), loss.backward(), etc."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"4. Network Pruning Techniques"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"Pruning removes redundant or insignificant parameters (weights, channels, or entire layers) from a neural network based on specific importance criteria, such as magnitude or gradient sensitivity. There are two primary types of pruning: Unstructured and Structured."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Unstructured Pruning: Sets individual weights to zero based on magnitude. Results in sparse matrices that often require specialized hardware acceleration to realize speedups."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Structured Pruning: Removes entire channels, filters, or attention heads. Yields a smaller, dense model directly compatible with standard hardware."},{"order":18,"type":"code","text":"import torch.nn.utils.prune as prune

# Apply L1 unstructured pruning to a linear layer
layer = nn.Linear(256, 128)
prune.l1_unstructured(layer, name="weight", amount=0.4)

# To make the pruning permanent and remove pruning masks
prune.remove(layer, "weight")"},{"order":19,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":20,"type":"paragraph","text":"Combining quantization and pruning provides a powerful pipeline for optimizing deep learning architectures. By removing redundant weights via pruning and compressing the representation via QAT or PTQ, engineers can deploy state-of-the-art models onto resource-constrained edge hardware with minimal loss in predictive accuracy."}]
